title: Metta Sutta Talk 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's talk emphasizes the importance of self-awareness, vulnerability, and letting go of ego, highlighting that sometimes stepping back can be more helpful than trying to control or dominate situations. This is reflected in the practice of metta (loving-kindness), which encourages cultivating peace and contentment by releasing attachment to material possessions and desires for status, and instead embracing a life of kindness and compassion towards all beings. By doing so, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and others, and cultivate a sense of unconditional love and support that brings joy and happiness to ourselves and those around us.
topics: Buddhist teachings on simplicity and detachment
Zen concept of "may all beings be happy"

*May all beings be happy.

So the idea is that this is the thought that naturally arises in you when you're living in the way it's describing.

No, you just feel nothing but love and support for everybody.

Happy sounds a little flip.
Words have power, and these are all words that translate from another language.
The actual line in Pali sounds something like this: *Sabe sata bhavantu sukitata.* Sabhi means all, the first word there means all, and the second word, sata, like satva, means beings.
So all beings, that's really literal.
The third word I said, bhavantu, means may they be.
So that's all good.
All beings may they be.
And the last word is a version of the word suka, which if you're a Buddhist geek, you may have heard of duka.
So this is the opposite of duka: suka, happiness.
Duka is suffering.
So may all beings be happy.
That seems like it is what it says.
But what kind of happiness are we talking about?
There's another word in Pali, piti, p-i-t-i, that means joy and delight.
So piti is the bubbly yippee, those exciting moments.

That's what we mean here.
So it's always translated as happy in English, but maybe it should be grounded joy.
I read one of the early Indian commentators said that piti, the other word, is the delight of getting something desirable.
Well, suka, the word here, is the savoring of it once you have it.
So it's a savoring of joy.
That sounds about right, huh?
So may all beings savor joy.
The real core idea in all of these teachings, and all of Buddhism really, is to notice how messed up we are by what you might call conditionality: if this, then that.
If you're nice to me, I'll be nice to you.
If I get what I want, then.
If only I had, then I could get, right?
It's all this conditional stuff.
And here our intention is to release from that.
Sometimes we talk about this, even in our very language, the idea that we have opposite words, like big and small, high and low, me and you.
It separates us, right?
We get separated and everything becomes conditional because we're separated.
And when we come together fully, then it's unconditional.
Of course, this is what's so great about wonderful moments of aesthetic art, wonderful moments of real love.
Those moments are unconditional, right?
You're just there.

So the healing of this is letting go of such ideas to where, not just like, "Okay, I'm not going to think that way," but where it doesn't make sense anymore.
Why would I think that way?
We are all beings who want to be happy and free from suffering, so naturally we love each other and we want to help each other out.

It's not your problem, even though I might think it is, if I'm separate.
So this is about the practice of unconditional love, actually.
